doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

title: "Riff Raff" and its comparison to Monk
summary: Gloria asks about his tune "Riff Raff"; Ware disputes Segal's Monk comparison.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: This was the first time you recorded 'Riff Raff' on the JG album, right?

That was your tune. And in the liner notes, when Joe Segal is talking about it, he says that this is reminiscent of (unintelligible) and then he talks about how these are the examples; why you were called the "Monk of the bass days" on this tune, Riff Raff.

Riff Raff? I can't see that. I don't believe that ... I don't know what he means by that. Riff Raff was just one of my ideas, and we run it over. And that was it. I had something to do with somebody else, I believe, in later years. After I played with him. But Leon Blevins had a part in that.

Well it could be then, I don't know how he means that, either, because he says that the flavor of the great Thelonious Monk permeates the proceedings of Riff Raff, and was most reminiscent of (inaudible) Well, You Needn't;"
Well, maybe he's talking in terms of the same kind of feel, you might say.
